title: Do less
hookLine: to be at peace, do few things, and only what's necessary (Meditations 4.24)
carry: ask who actually needs me now
last: AN HONEST ANSWER IN AN EMPTY ROOM.

cards: Look at your to-do list. Not the written one, the one in your head. Reply to that.
Look into this. Weigh in on the group chat. Have an opinion about the news.
Check the thing you already checked. It's long, and it's hard to say which items actually matter.
Marcus Aurelius had more on his plate than most, and in the twenty-fourth entry of book four he passed on an old piece of advice that sounds almost like permission. Today: do less.

teach.h: DO FEW THINGS, SAYS THE PHILOSOPHER.
teach.b: Do few things, says the philosopher, if you want to be at peace. Marcus doesn't name him. Readers usually identify him as Democritus, an earlier Greek thinker who wrote about cheerful calm.

teach.h: DO WHAT'S NECESSARY, AND DO IT WELL.
teach.b: Wouldn't it be better, he asks, to say: do what's necessary, and what the reason of a social creature requires, and in the way it requires?
That brings a double peace: the peace of doing things well, and the peace of doing few. Not just fewer. Fewer and better.
Then the hard sentence. Most of what we say and do, Marcus writes, isn't necessary. Take it away, and you'll have more leisure and less disturbance.

teach.h: IS THIS ONE OF THE UNNECESSARY THINGS?
teach.b: So at every moment, ask: is this one of the unnecessary things? And he goes a step deeper.
Cut the unnecessary thoughts, he says, and the unnecessary actions that follow them won't happen either. The extra reply starts as an extra thought. The extra worry starts as one more what-if.
This isn't laziness. It's triage. A doctor in a crowded room doesn't treat everyone at once; she asks who actually needs her now.
Do less isn't a mood. It's a question, asked often, with an honest answer.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the question from Meditations 4.24, 'is this one of the unnecessary things?', to trim their lists and their replies.

o: doing only what's necessary, and doing it well
saying no to every request so you can protect your time
resting more and working less, whatever needs doing

p: do few things, to be at peace
do what's necessary, and do it well

s: 'do few things' is Marcus's own saying
he's quoting an earlier philosopher, usually taken to be Democritus, then improving on it.
Marcus says most of what we say and do isn't necessary
take it away, he says, and you'll have more leisure and less disturbance.
Marcus says to cut unnecessary thoughts as well as acts
so the unnecessary acts that follow them won't happen.

games.q: a heated thread at work doesn't involve you. you have a sharp reply ready. what fits Meditations 4.24?
o: ask whether it's necessary, and let it go.
post it, then explain it later.
games.why: Marcus: at every moment ask, is this one of the unnecessary things? the reply that isn't needed never needs sending.

practice: Go through today's list, written or unwritten, one item at a time, and ask Marcus's question of each: is this necessary? Some are, and some clearly aren't; pick one that isn't, and cross it off, on paper or in your mind.
Notice what happens, if anything, when it goes.

wordCard.voice: Do less. Marcus takes an old philosopher's advice, do few things, and sharpens it: do what's necessary, do it well, and drop the rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'good spirits, cheerful calm': the theme of the writing usually linked to 'do few things'; not a word from 4.24 itself.

carryVoice: Your line: ask who actually needs me now. Fewer things, done better. Day five hundred fifty-eight, done.
